title: HTTP Server
subtitle: Building web servers with Node's built-in http module
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Web servers handle HTTP requests and return responses. Understanding the low-level http module helps you understand what frameworks like Express do under the hood.
whyItExists.solution: http.createServer() creates a server. The callback receives (req, res) — a request object with method, URL, headers, and body; and a response object to write status, headers, and the response body.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Learning the fundamentals, writing minimal microservices, or situations where Express overhead is undesirable. In production, most teams use Express or Fastify.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For real applications with routing, middleware, authentication — use Express or Fastify rather than re-implementing those features yourself.

explainModes.beginner: http.createServer() creates a web server. When a browser requests a page, your callback function runs with the request details (what URL, what method) and a response object. You call res.end('Hello') to send back a response.
explainModes.simple: const server = http.createServer((req, res) => { res.writeHead(200, {'Content-Type':'text/plain'}); res.end('Hello'); }); server.listen(3000). req.method: GET/POST/etc. req.url: the path. req.headers: request headers. Reading body: req is a stream — collect chunks. res.writeHead(statusCode, headers). res.write(chunk). res.end(data). JSON API: set Content-Type: application/json and JSON.stringify the response.
explainModes.standard: Routing: check req.url and req.method — a switch or if/else tree. Body reading: POST/PUT bodies come as a stream. Collect: let body=''; req.on('data', chunk => body += chunk); req.on('end', () => { const data = JSON.parse(body); }). CORS headers: res.setHeader('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*'). Error handling: unhandled errors in the callback crash the server — wrap in try/catch. Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error.
explainModes.technical: Keep-alive connections: HTTP/1.1 reuses TCP connections by default. Each request/response cycle is one req/res pair on the same connection. server.keepAliveTimeout controls idle timeout. http.Agent: manages a connection pool for outgoing requests (http.request). For incoming, Node manages this automatically. HTTPS: use the https module (same API as http) with key/cert options. TLS termination is more commonly done at a load balancer (Nginx, AWS ALB) in production.
explainModes.deepDive: Backpressure: if the client reads slower than you write, res.write() returns false — wait for 'drain' before writing more. Node's http module handles this automatically for most use cases. HTTP/2: Node 18+ has a stable http2 module — multiplexed streams over one TCP connection. Express 5 supports HTTP/2 via the spdy adapter. QUIC/HTTP3: experimental in Node. Undici: Node's modern HTTP client — faster than the built-in http module for outgoing requests, now backing fetch() in Node 18+.

content.text: In real Node.js, reading the request body requires collecting stream chunks: `let body=''; req.on('data', c => body+=c); req.on('end', () => JSON.parse(body))`. The sandbox simplifies this by providing req.body as a string directly.

questions.question: What are the `req` and `res` objects in an http.createServer callback?
options: req is the HTML request string; res is an array of response strings
req (IncomingMessage) contains the request data (method, url, headers, body stream); res (ServerResponse) is used to write the status code, headers, and body back to the client
req and res are both EventEmitters with no special HTTP methods
req is synchronous; res is asynchronous
questions.explanation: req is an IncomingMessage (a Readable stream): it has .method, .url, .headers, and emits 'data'/'end' events for the request body. res is a ServerResponse (a Writable stream): call res.writeHead(statusCode, headers) to set the response head, then res.end(body) or res.write(chunk) to send the body. Once you call res.end(), the response is complete and the connection is ready for the next request.

faq.q: Why do most Node.js projects use Express instead of the raw http module?
faq.a: The raw http module handles every detail manually: routing (if/else on req.url), body parsing (stream chunks), content negotiation, error handling, middleware chains. Express adds routing (app.get('/path', handler)), automatic body parsing (express.json()), middleware (app.use()), and cleaner error handling — saving hundreds of lines of boilerplate for every real API.
